fixes.replace: How are the savings from an efficiency upgrade checked after commissioning?

fixes.find: Utility and manufacturer programs change from year to year, so these questions belong before equipment is ordered. Three are worth asking. Does the program cover high-efficiency equipment, controls and commissioning? Is pre-approval required before installation? What proof of the installed model and its rating does the application need? Amounts are left out here because program terms move.
fixes.replace: Savings are checked by comparing energy use before and after the work on the same basis. That needs a baseline of utility bills across the seasons, adjusted for weather, operating hours, occupancy and rate changes. Controls deserve a second look some weeks after commissioning, because overrides and schedule edits can quietly undo the result. Where an incentive program sets its own measurement rules, those rules decide what counts. A lower bill alone does not prove the HVAC change worked, and a higher one does not prove it failed. A proposal should state which inputs its savings estimate used, so the follow-up comparison tests the same assumptions.
fixes.why: MAJOR 2 + length: duplicate rebate answer replaced with a distinct measurement-and-verification answer (general guidance only)

fixes.find: Zoning fixes a distribution problem, not a capacity problem. In long Chicago storefronts and converted loft floors, one thermostat reads one spot. The far end runs warm or cold, staff override the setpoint, and the system works harder. Adding capacity makes that worse. The fix is dampers and separate control zones where the duct layout allows, and ductless mini-splits where it does not.
fixes.replace: Zoning can help when the problem is distribution rather than capacity, but it is not an automatic cure. Uneven temperature can also come from the building envelope, a changed load, too little capacity, control settings or the duct layout, so the cause needs diagnosing first. In long Chicago storefronts and converted loft floors, one thermostat reads one spot. The far end runs warm or cold, staff override the setpoint, and the system works harder. Where distribution is the cause, adding capacity tends to make that worse. The fix may then be dampers and separate control zones where the duct layout allows, or ductless mini-splits where it does not. City & Suburban diagnoses before anything is quoted.
fixes.why: MAJOR 3 + length: zoning qualified; envelope, load, capacity, controls and distribution named as possible causes

fixes.find: Controls are the least expensive lever and the one most often left on a factory schedule. A connected thermostat saves energy only when its schedule matches the hours a space is used. Schedules, setbacks and lockouts should be set at commissioning and written down. A building then stops heating empty offices at 2 a.m. Many commercial setups still run the default schedule from the day of installation.
fixes.replace: Controls can be a lower-cost lever, and they are often left on a factory schedule. Cost and effect depend on compatibility with the existing equipment and the installation scope, and an inexpensive change is not always enough. A connected thermostat saves energy only when its schedule matches the hours a space is used. Schedules, setbacks and lockouts should be set at commissioning and written down. A building then stops heating empty offices at 2 a.m. Many commercial setups still run the default schedule from the day of installation. Measured energy use before and after the change is the fair test of any savings claim.
fixes.why: MAJOR 4 + length: universal cost ordering removed; compatibility, scope and measured savings compared
